catalog_quote: [p.171] Although significant variation pervaded early descriptions of Hadza prosody, Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone polarity (see Section 6.3). Contour tones—LH rising and HL falling—only occur on (bimoraic) long vowels, composed of two level tones on separate tone bearing moras. ... Although tone in Hadza is lexically contrastive, its functional load is relatively low in roots. [p.158] ... lengthening morphemes prompted Sands (2013b:117) to analyze them as causing stress shift. However, this thesis does not find stress in Hadza. [p.165] Hadza is a tone language, defined as a language “in which an indication of pitch enters into the lexical realization of at least some morphemes” (Hyman 2001b:1367; Hyman 2006:229), contrasting both lexical tone and grammatical tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [p.171] Although significant variation pervaded early descriptions of Hadza prosody, Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone polarity (see Section 6.3). [p.158] These vowel lengthening morphemes prompted Sands (2013b:117) to analyze them as causing stress shift. However, this thesis does not find stress in Hadza.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (the our source list 'held' list is empty but the directory exists with , , the WPP 84 volume PDF, its Hadza scanned text and two page pins, and). (1) Coburn 2024, extracted text: p.183 carries printed page number 171 and heading '6.2 Basics of Hadza tone'; the sentences 'Although significant variation pervaded early descriptions of Hadza prosody, Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone pol…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hadza is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language with the mora as tone-bearing unit and all H/L combinations attested on roots of 1-3 moras; the author explicitly finds no word stress (earlier 'stress'/'stress shift' observations are reanalysed as tone plus morphological vowel lengthening). The older instrumental description (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996:178) instead called the system unclear and 'best accounted for by analysing Hadza as a pitch accent language, with prominence shifting from one syllable to another according to the context', noting high-toned syllables are longer and more stressed and word melodies LHL / HL.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Coburn denies stress altogether. (Berger 1943, per Coburn p.167, marked 'stronger' and 'weaker' dynamic accents without analysis.)
new_statements.exceptions: No stress rule, hence no exceptions. Tonal notes: contour tones restricted to bimoraic long vowels; toneless suffixes/enclitics take polar tone; automatic downstep (HLH -> HLM); tonal functional load in roots is low.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root + affix) tonal analysis from elicited citation and frame forms ('Is a ___' copular frame, imperative verb forms); Sands et al. 1996 explicitly say prominence shifts with context and that interaction with larger prosodic constituents was not worked out.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe Hadza as spoken in the Mang'ola / Lake Eyasi area (Coburn 2024: fieldwork 2022 with speakers from several areas; Sands et al. 1996: Mang'ola consultants). No dialect split is relevant; glottocode hadz1240 applies directly.

tone_statements.citation: Harvey, Andrew, Richard Griscom & Jeremy Coburn. In press (submitted 2024). A Sketch of Hadza Grammar. Studies in African Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: Hadza is a tone language with two tone levels: High (H) versus Low (L), where the mora is the tone-bearing unit (TBU). Additionally, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive their tonal specification only via tonal phonological processes, as described below. ... Contour tones occur on long (bimoraic) vowels, which may bear any combination of H and L, i.e., HH, HL, LH, and LL. ... The HL falling tone contour, however, is only found lexically on a few roots. Although tone is lexically contrastive, it carries a relatively low functional load in roots.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H/L, mora = TBU; long vowels bear HH, HL, LH, LL sequences; select suffixes/enclitics toneless, filled by tone polarity (after Coburn 2024); minimal pairs given; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone polarity (see Section 6.3). tone_statements.locator: sec. 6.2 'Basics of Hadza tone', p. 171; polarity statement sec. 6.3.3 p. 184-185
tone_statements.summary: H vs L on moras; contours = level sequences on long vowels; only automatic downstep (HLH -> HLM). Toneless plural suffixes -beʔe/-biʔi and copula =pʰeʔe/=pʰiʔi take tone polar to stem-final tone.

tone_statements.citation: Coburn, Jeremy, Bonny Sands, Andrew Harvey & Richard Griscom. Forthcoming. Tonal patterns of Hadza nouns. In Proceedings of the 10th World Congress of African Linguistics (WOCAL 10).
tone_statements.quote: In this paper, we present a new analysis of Hadza tonology. In previous work, tone has been considered a property of the syllable (Sands 2013, Tucker et al. 1977), whereas we will argue that the mora is the tone-bearing unit. Based on data collected in 2019 and 2020 from four different Hadza-speaking areas, we argue that morae may be specified for H tone or unspecified (which are realized with low tone). In addition to presenting a typology of tone patterns in Hadza roots, we will also present a typology of the prominence patterns seen.
tone_statements.summary: Privative H vs toneless (surface low) on moras; root tone-pattern typology and -ko H/low alternation by phrase position announced but not given; no consonant-tone restrictions.
